claims.claim: The Arctic ecotype does not show circalunar or circadian rhythms (Pflüger and Neumann, 1971).
claims.source: It does not show circalunar or circadian rhythms (Pflüger and Neumann, 1971).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature and is consistent with the emergence data in Figure 1.

claims.claim: The geological history of Northern Europe (Patton et al., 2017) implies the Baltic Sea and the high Arctic could only be colonized by Clunio after the last glacial ice shield regressed about 10,000 years ago.
claims.source: The geological history of Northern Europe (Patton et al., 2017) implies the Baltic Sea and the high Arctic could only be colonized by Clunio after the last glacial ice shield regressed about 10,000 years ago.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature on geological history.

claims.claim: Subfossil Clunio head capsules in Baltic Sea sediment cores support the inference that colonization occurred after ice shield regression (Hofmann and Winn, 2000).
claims.source: This inference is also supported by subfossil Clunio head capsules in Baltic Sea sediment cores (Hofmann and Winn, 2000).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claims.claim: The new adaptations to the absence of tides in the Baltic Sea and to polar day in the high Arctic must have occurred within the last 10,000 years.
claims.source: The new adaptations to the absence of tides in the Baltic Sea and to polar day in the high Arctic must therefore have occurred within this time frame.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference based on the timing of postglacial colonization.

claims.claim: Laboratory strains were established from field collections at multiple sites including Tromsø, Bergen, Sehlendorf, Ar, Helgoland, and Port-en-Bessin.
claims.source: Starting from field work in Northern Europe (Figure 1A), we established one laboratory strain of the Arctic ecotype from Tromsø (Norway, Tro-tAR; see methods for strain nomenclature) and three laboratory strains of the Baltic ecotype, from Bergen (Norway, Ber-2AR), Sehlendorf (Germany; Seh-2AR) and Ar (Sweden; Ar-2AR). We also established a strain of the Atlantic ecotype from Bergen (Ber-1SL, sympatric with Ber-2AR) and used two existing Atlantic ecotype laboratory strains from Helgoland (Germany; He-1SL) and Port-en-Bessin (France; Por-1SL).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the methods used to establish laboratory strains.

claims.claim: The identity of the ecotypes was confirmed in the laboratory by the absence of a lunar rhythm in the Baltic and Arctic ecotypes.
claims.source: We confirmed the identity of the ecotypes in the laboratory by the absence of a lunar rhythm in the Baltic and Arctic ecotypes (Figure 1B–H), their circadian rhythm (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–H) and their oviposition behavior (for details see methods section).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the emergence data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The Baltic ecotype from Bergen (Ber-2AR) was found weakly lunar-rhythmic.
claims.source: The Baltic ecotype from Bergen (Ber-2AR, Figure 1F) was found weakly lunar-rhythmic.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the emergence data shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: 168 field-caught individuals from six geographic sites were sequenced for full nuclear and mitochondrial genomes.
claims.source: We sequenced the full nuclear and mitochondrial genomes of 168 field-caught individuals from six geographic sites, including the two sympatric population ecotypes from Bergen (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the genomic data collection.

claims.claim: Principal component analysis based on 792,032 SNPs separates populations by geographic location rather than ecotype.
claims.source: Based on a set of 792,032 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), we first investigated population structure and evolutionary history by performing a principal component analysis (PCA; Figure 2A–B) and testing for genetic admixture (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the PCA results shown in Figure 2A-B.

claims.claim: There is strong geographic isolation between populations from different sites.
claims.source: First, there is strong geographic isolation between populations from different sites. In PCA, clusters are formed according to geography (Figure 2A–B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1). Mitochondrial haplotypes are not shared and are diagnostically different between geographic sites (Figure 2D). In ADMIXTURE, the optimal number of genetic groups is six (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2), corresponding to the number of geographic sites, and there is basically no mixing between the six clusters (Figure 2C; K=6). Finally, there is isolation by distance (IBD; Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by PCA (Figure 2A-B), mitochondrial haplotype network (Figure 2D), ADMIXTURE analysis (Figure 2C), and isolation by distance analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).

claims.claim: The sympatric ecotypes in Bergen are genetically very similar.
claims.source: Second, the sympatric ecotypes in Bergen are genetically very similar. In PCA they are not separated in the first four principal components (Figure 2A–B) and they are the only populations that share mitochondrial haplotypes (Figure 2D). In the ADMIXTURE analysis, they are only distinguished at K=7, a value larger than the optimal K. As soon as the two populations are distinguished, some individuals show signals of admixed origin (Figure 2C; K=7), compatible with the assumption of ongoing gene flow and incomplete reproductive isolation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by PCA (Figure 2A-B), mitochondrial haplotype network (Figure 2D), and ADMIXTURE analysis (Figure 2C).

claims.claim: The genetic similarity between sympatric ecotypes in Bergen questions the species status of C. balticus.
claims.source: These observations question the species status of C. balticus, which was based on the assumption of temporal isolation between these two populations (Heimbach, 1978).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic data showing similarity between the sympatric ecotypes.

claims.claim: After the ice age, Clunio colonized northern Europe from a single source and expanded along two fronts into the Baltic Sea and into the high Arctic.
claims.source: Third, the data suggest that after the ice age Clunio colonized northern Europe from a single source and expanded along two fronts into the Baltic Sea and into the high Arctic. The mitochondrial haplotype network expands from a single center, which implies a quick radiation from a colonizing haplotype (Figure 2D; note that all sampled populations occur in areas under a former ice shield cover). There is also a large degree of shared nuclear polymorphisms. Thirty-four percent of polymorphic SNPs are polymorphic in all seven populations and 93% are polymorphic in at least two populations (Figure 2—figure supplement 4). Separation of the Baltic Sea populations along PC1 and the Arctic population along PC2 (Figure 2A), suggests that Clunio expanded into the high Arctic and into the Baltic Sea independently. Congruently, nucleotide diversity significantly decreases toward both expansion fronts (Figure 2—figure supplement 5, Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the mitochondrial haplotype network (Figure 2D), shared polymorphisms (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), PCA (Figure 2A), and nucleotide diversity patterns (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).

claims.claim: Postglacial establishment from a common source indicates that the Baltic and Arctic ecotypes have evolved their new local adaptations in less than 10,000 years.
claims.source: Postglacial establishment from a common source indicates that the Baltic and Arctic ecotypes have evolved their new local adaptations during this expansion time, that is, in less than 10,000 years.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of postglacial colonization and the genetic data.

claims.claim: ADMIXTURE analysis reveals that sympatric co-existence of the Atlantic and Baltic ecotypes in Bergen likely results from introgression of Baltic ecotype individuals into an existing Atlantic ecotype population.
claims.source: Fourth, ADMIXTURE analysis reveals that sympatric co-existence of the Atlantic and Baltic ecotypes in Bergen likely results from introgression of Baltic ecotype individuals into an existing Atlantic ecotype population. At K=2 and K=3 the two Baltic Sea populations Seh-2AR and Ar-2AR are separated from all other populations and the two Bergen populations Ber-2AR and Ber-1SL show a marked genetic contribution coming from these Baltic Sea populations (Figure 2C). The Baltic genetic component is slightly larger for the Baltic ecotype Ber-2AR population than for the Atlantic ecotype Ber-1SL population.
claims.evidence: This is supported by ADMIXTURE analysis (Figure 2C) and TreeMix analysis (Figure 2E).

claims.claim: TreeMix detects predominantly an introgression from Seh-2AR into Ber-2AR.
claims.source: A statistical analysis via TreeMix detects predominantly an introgression from Seh-2AR into Ber-2AR (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplements 6 and 7), suggesting that haplotypes that convey the Baltic ecotype have introgressed into a population of Atlantic ecotype, resulting in the now observed sympatric co-existence of Baltic and Atlantic ecotypes in Bergen.
claims.evidence: This is supported by TreeMix analysis (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplements 6 and 7).

claims.claim: Tree topologies change rapidly along the chromosomes, indicating massive sharing of haplotypes across populations.
claims.source: We found that tree topologies change rapidly along the chromosomes (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 2). The tree topology obtained for the entire genome (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) dominates only in few genomic windows (Figure 3A, black bars 'Orig.'), while usually one or several other topologies account for more than 75% of the tree topologies (Figure 3A, gray bars 'Misc.'). Hardly ever do all combinations of six individuals follow a single population tree topology (Figure 3A, stars), which implies that in most genomic windows some individuals do not group with their population. Taken together, this indicates a massive sharing of haplotypes across populations.
claims.evidence: This is supported by topology weighting analysis (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claims.claim: The genome-wide f4 ratio was –0.00062 (standard error 0.00008) and was found to be significantly different from 0, indicating some degree of introgression.
claims.source: The genome-wide f4 ratio was –0.00062 (standard error 0.00008) and by comparison to coalescent simulations was found to be significantly different from 0, indicating some degree of introgression. However, the signature of introgression was driven by only 775 SNPs, which is only 0.17% of the total dataset. Thus, the largest part of haplotype sharing can be explained by incomplete lineage sorting, typical for such radiation situations.
claims.evidence: This is supported by f4 ratio test analysis.

claims.claim: The degree of lunar rhythmicity segregates within and between crossing families, suggesting a heterogeneous multi-genic basis of lunar arrhythmicity.
claims.source: Interestingly, the degree of lunar rhythmicity segregates within and between crossing families (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting a heterogeneous multi-genic basis of lunar arrhythmicity.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the crossing data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Genetic segregation in the cross implies that the weak rhythm observed in Ber-2AR is due to genetic polymorphism.
claims.source: Genetic segregation in the cross implies that the weak rhythm observed in Ber-2AR is due to genetic polymorphism. The Ber-2AR strain seems to carry some lunar-rhythmic alleles, likely due to gene flow from the sympatric Atlantic ecotype (see Figure 1C and results below).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the crossing data and the weak lunar rhythm observed in Ber-2AR.

claims.claim: QTL analysis did not reveal any significant QTL for lunar rhythmicity.
claims.source: However, QTL analysis with various algorithms did not reveal any significant QTL for lunar rhythmicity (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the QTL mapping results shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The sex determining locus was clearly detectable in QTL mapping, confirming sufficient power for QTL detection.
claims.source: As a control that in principle we had sufficient power for QTL mapping in this crossing family, we also mapped the sex determining locus, which was clearly detectable (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the QTL mapping results shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Lunar rhythmicity is not controlled by a single large-effect locus, but rather has an oligogenic or possibly even polygenic basis.
claims.source: We can conclude that lunar rhythmicity is not controlled by a single large-effect locus, but rather has an oligogenic or possibly even polygenic basis.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of significant QTL for lunar rhythmicity despite sufficient power to detect the sex-determining locus.

claims.claim: Overly differentiated variants and ecotype-associated variants were detected all over the genome, but many were concentrated in the middle of the telocentric chromosome 1.
claims.source: Overly differentiated variants (XtX statistic; Figure 3B) and ecotype-associated variants ecotype (eBPmc; Figure 3C) were detected all over the genome, but many were concentrated in the middle of the telocentric chromosome 1.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the genome-wide association analysis shown in Figure 3B-C.

claims.claim: Tests for association of variants with environmental variables such as sea surface temperature or salinity find fewer associated SNPs and no concentration on chromosome 1.
claims.source: Tests for association of variants with environmental variables such as sea surface temperature or salinity find fewer associated SNPs and no concentration on chromosome 1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D–E), confirming that the detected signals are not due to general genome properties, but are specific to the ecotypes.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the association analysis with environmental variables shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3D-E.

claims.claim: Genetic differentiation was particularly low in the Ber-1SL vs. Ber-2AR comparison.
claims.source: The distributions of FST values in all pairwise population comparisons confirmed that genetic differentiation was particularly low in the Ber-1SL vs. Ber-2AR comparison (Figure 3—figure supplements 4 and 5).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the FST distributions shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 4 and 5.

claims.claim: There is not a single diagnostic variant (FST = 1) between Baltic and Atlantic ecotypes, and even variants with FST ≥ 0.75 are very rare (n=63).
claims.source: Notably, when assessing genetic differentiation of Baltic vs Atlantic ecotype (72 vs 72 individuals; Figure 3E; Figure 3—figure supplement 6), there is not a single diagnostic variant (FST = 1), and even variants with FST ≥ 0.75 are very rare (n=63; Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the FST analysis shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claims.claim: The cluster of ecotype-associated variants on chromosome 1 overlaps with three large blocks of long-range linkage disequilibrium.
claims.source: The cluster of ecotype-associated variants on chromosome 1 overlaps with three large blocks of long-range linkage disequilibrium (LD; Figure 3—figure supplement 8).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the LD analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 8.

claims.claim: LD blocks are not ecotype-specific.
claims.source: However, the boundaries of the LD blocks do not correspond to the ecotype-associated region and differ between populations. LD blocks are not ecotype-specific.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the LD analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 8.

claims.claim: Local PCA of the strongly ecotype associated region does not reveal patterns consistent with a chromosomal inversion or another segregating structural variant.
claims.source: Local PCA of the strongly ecotype associated region does not reveal patterns consistent with a chromosomal inversion or another segregating structural variant (Figure 3—figure supplement 9).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the local PCA analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 9.

claims.claim: Genetic differentiation is not generally elevated in the ecotype-associated cluster on chromosome 1, but drops to baseline levels in between ecotype-associated loci.
claims.source: Notably, genetic differentiation is not generally elevated in the ecotype-associated cluster on chromosome 1, as would be expected for a segregating structural variant, but drops to baseline levels in between ecotype-associated loci (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the FST analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Numerous genomic loci – inside and outside the cluster on chromosome 1 – are associated with ecological adaptation and none of these are differentially fixed between ecotypes.
claims.source: Taken together, these observations imply that numerous genomic loci – inside and outside the cluster on chromosome 1 – are associated with ecological adaptation and none of these are differentially fixed between ecotypes.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the genomic data showing many ecotype-associated loci with no fixed differences.

claims.claim: The genomic data virtually exclude the possibility that only one or few loci have driven the new ecotype formation, suggesting instead that ecotype formation is based on a complex polygenic architecture.
claims.source: In line with QTL mapping, this virtually excludes the possibility that only one or few loci have driven the new ecotype formation, suggesting instead that ecotype formation is based on a complex polygenic architecture.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the genomic data and QTL mapping results.

claims.claim: 82% of the ecotype-associated SNPs are polymorphic in both Atlantic and Baltic ecotypes, suggesting that the largest part of ecotype-associated alleles originates from standing genetic variation.
claims.source: Based on this comparison, we found that 82% of the ecotype-associated SNPs are polymorphic in both Atlantic and Baltic ecotypes, suggesting that the largest part of ecotype-associated alleles originates from standing genetic variation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the analysis of shared polymorphisms among ecotype-associated SNPs.

claims.claim: 90% of the alleles associated with the Northern European ecotypes are also segregating in at least one of the southern populations (Vigo and St. Jean-de-Luz), supporting the notion that adaptation in the North involves a re-assortment of existing standing genetic variation.
claims.source: We found that 90% of the alleles associated with the Northern European ecotypes are also segregating in at least one of these southern populations, supporting the notion that adaptation in the North involves a re-assortment of existing standing genetic variation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the comparison with published population resequencing data from southern populations.

claims.claim: The vast majority of ecotype-specific variants are classified as intergenic modifier variants, suggesting that ecotype formation might primarily rely on regulatory mutations.
claims.source: The vast majority of ecotype-specific variants are classified as intergenic modifier variants, suggesting that ecotype formation might primarily rely on regulatory mutations.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the SnpEff analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 11.

claims.claim: GO term enrichment analysis suggests that ecological adaptation prominently involves the circadian clock, supported by three of the top four GO terms.
claims.source: GO term enrichment analysis suggests that ecological adaptation prominently involves the circadian clock, supported by three of the top four GO terms (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the GO term enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Clustering of genes and GO terms reveals two dominant signatures: many GO terms are associated with circadian timing and are driven by a small number of genes, which include almost all core circadian clock genes; and almost half of the genes are annotated with biological processes involved in nervous system development.
claims.source: Clustering the resulting table by genes and GO terms reveals two dominant signatures (Figure 5B). Many GO terms are associated with circadian timing and are driven by a small number of genes, which include almost all core circadian clock genes (Figure 5B and C). As a second strong signal, almost half of the genes are annotated with biological processes involved in nervous system development (Figure 5B and C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the gene-GO term clustering analysis shown in Figure 5B-C.

claims.claim: GO term enrichment is also found for ecdysteroid metabolism, imaginal disc development, and gonad development.
claims.source: GO term enrichment is also found for ecdysteroid metabolism, imaginal disc development, and gonad development (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the GO term enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: There is a striking absence of GO terms involved in metabolic processes or immune system processes.
claims.source: There is a striking absence of GO terms involved in metabolic processes or immune system processes, despite these GO terms being annotated to 2634 genes or 185 genes, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the GO term enrichment analysis.

claims.claim: The detected GO terms are highly consistent with the known ecotype differences and suggest that ecotypes are mainly defined by changes in the circadian clock and nervous system development.
claims.source: Taken together, the detected GO terms are highly consistent with the known ecotype differences and suggest that ecotypes are mainly defined by changes in the circadian clock and nervous system development.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the GO term enrichment analysis and known ecotype characteristics.

claims.claim: GO terms 'male courtship behavior', 'inter-male aggression' and 'copulation' highlight a previously unknown aspect of Clunio ecotype formation.
claims.source: A previously unknown aspect of Clunio ecotype formation is highlighted by the GO terms 'male courtship behavior', 'inter-male aggression' and 'copulation' (Figure 5). These processes are subject to sexual selection and considered to evolve rapidly. They could in the long term entail assortative mating between ecotypes.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the GO term enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: 13 genes in 8 distinct genomic regions are strongly differentiated between ecotypes (FST ≥ 0.75) and highly ecotype-associated (eBPmc >10).
claims.source: As a second line of evidence, we therefore selected variants with the highest ecotype-association by increasing the eBPmc cut-off to 10. This reduced the set of affected genes from 1,400 to 69 (Supplementary files 9 and 10). Additionally, we only considered genes with variants that are strongly differentiated between the ecotypes (FST ≥ 0.75, compare Figure 3E), leaving 13 genes in 8 distinct genomic regions (Figure 6A; numbered in Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the candidate gene analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: All major biological processes detected in GO term analysis are also reflected in the strongly ecotype-associated loci.
claims.source: In summary, only two out of the top 13 ecotype-associated genes were included in the top 40 GO terms (Figure 6A). Nevertheless, all major biological processes detected in GO term analysis (Figure 5) are also reflected in the strongly ecotype-associated loci (Figure 6), giving a robust signal that circadian timing, sensory perception and nervous system development are underlying ecotype formation in C. marinus.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the comparison of GO term enrichment (Figure 5) and candidate gene analysis (Figure 6).

claims.claim: Despite the top 13 loci being the most differentiated between ecotypes in the entire genome, there is at best a mild reduction in genetic diversity and a mild increase in LD.
claims.source: Finally, we assessed the top 13 strongly ecotype-associated loci for signatures of selective sweeps in genetic diversity and LD (Figure 6B–G). Despite these loci being the most differentiated between ecotypes in the entire genome, there is at best a mild reduction in genetic diversity and a mild increase in LD (Figure 6B–G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the analysis of genetic diversity and LD at candidate loci shown in Figure 6B-G.

claims.claim: If selection acted on these loci, it must have been very soft, underscoring a history of polygenic adaptation from standing genetic variation and continued recombination.
claims.source: If selection acted on these loci, it must have been very soft, underscoring a history of polygenic adaptation from standing genetic variation and continued recombination.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of strong selective sweep signatures at the most differentiated loci.

claims.claim: The deep genomic analysis of Clunio populations allowed reconstruction of a detailed biogeographic history of their different ecotypes.
claims.source: The deep genomic analysis of Clunio populations has allowed us to reconstruct a detailed biogeographic history of their different ecotypes.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement about the results of the study.

claims.claim: The two sympatric ecotypes that were considered different species turned out to be the most closely related populations in the sample.
claims.source: Most surprisingly, the two sympatric ecotypes that were considered different species turned out to be the most closely related populations in the sample, testifying the high power of ecology in generating differential adaptation in the face of gene flow.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the genetic similarity between Ber-1SL and Ber-2AR shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: While ecotype-associated alleles differ in allele frequency, they are largely shared between ecotypes, which suggests that adaptation primarily involves standing genetic variation from many different loci.
claims.source: We found that while ecotype-associated alleles differ in allele frequency, they are largely shared between ecotypes, which suggests that adaptation primarily involves standing genetic variation from many different loci.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the analysis of shared polymorphisms among ecotype-associated alleles.

claims.claim: A similar re-use of existing regulatory variation has been found in ecotype formation in sticklebacks (Chan et al., 2010; Kingman, 2020; Verta and Jones, 2019) or mimicry in Heliconius butterflies (Edelman et al., 2019).
claims.source: A similar re-use of existing regulatory variation has been found in ecotype formation in sticklebacks Chan et al., 2010; Kingman, 2020; Verta and Jones, 2019 or mimicry in Heliconius butterflies Edelman et al., 2019.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claims.claim: In Heliconius, alleles are shared over large evolutionary distances via introgression, while Clunio ecotypes diverged recently from a common source.
claims.source: However, while in Heliconius alleles are shared over large evolutionary distances via introgression, Clunio ecotypes diverged recently from a common source, as is illustrated by massive and genome-wide shared polymorphism.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison between Clunio and Heliconius based on the data presented in this study and published literature.

claims.claim: The ancestral Atlantic ecotype comprises many genetically determined circadian timing types that are adapted to the local tides (Kaiser, 2014; Neumann, 1967; Kaiser et al., 2016; Kaiser et al., 2021).
claims.source: The ancestral Atlantic ecotype comprises many genetically determined circadian timing types that are adapted to the local tides (Kaiser, 2014; Neumann, 1967; Kaiser et al., 2016; Kaiser et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claims.claim: Existing genetic variants conveying emergence at dusk were likely selected or re-assorted to form the Baltic ecotype's highly concentrated emergence at dusk.
claims.source: Existing genetic variants conveying emergence at dusk were likely selected or re-assorted to form the Baltic ecotype's highly concentrated emergence at dusk.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the known variation in the Atlantic ecotype and the observed phenotype of the Baltic ecotype.

claims.claim: Good congruence between known phenotypic differences and detected biological processes could be a hallmark of polygenic adaptation.
claims.source: We propose that good congruence between known phenotypic differences and detected biological processes could be a hallmark of polygenic adaptation, as only polygenic adaptation is expected to leave a footprint in many genes of the same ecologically relevant biological process.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical proposition based on the results of this study.

claims.claim: Clunio's circalunar clock is known to tightly regulate ecdysteroid-dependent development and maturation just prior to pupation (Neumann and Spindler, 1991).
claims.source: Firstly, Clunio's circalunar clock is known to tightly regulate ecdysteroid-dependent development and maturation just prior to pupation (Neumann and Spindler, 1991).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claims.claim: Lunar arrhythmicity may rely on an escape of developmental processes from circalunar clock control.
claims.source: Lunar arrhythmicity may rely on an escape of these processes from circalunar clock control.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the GO term enrichment for ecdysteroid metabolism and imaginal disc development.

claims.claim: It has been hypothesized that circalunar clocks involve a circadian clock (Bünning and Müller, 1961) and such a mechanism has been experimentally confirmed in the midge Pontomyia oceana (Soong and Chang, 2012).
claims.source: Secondly, it has been hypothesized that circalunar clocks involve a circadian clock (Bünning and Müller, 1961) and such a mechanism has been experimentally confirmed in the midge Pontomyia oceana (Soong and Chang, 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claims.claim: The overwhelming circadian signal in the data might be responsible for both circadian timing adaptations and the loss of circalunar rhythms.
claims.source: Thus, the overwhelming circadian signal in our data might be responsible for both circadian timing adaptations and the loss of circalunar rhythms.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the GO term enrichment for circadian clock genes.

claims.claim: Clunio's circalunar clock is synchronized with the external lunar cycle via moonlight, as well as tidal cycles of water turbulence and temperature (Neumann, 2014).
claims.source: Thirdly, Clunio's circalunar clock is synchronized with the external lunar cycle via moonlight, as well as tidal cycles of water turbulence and temperature (Neumann, 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claims.claim: Sensory receptor development, wiring or sensitivity might differ between ecotypes.
claims.source: Our data suggests that sensory receptor development, wiring or sensitivity might differ between ecotypes.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the GO term enrichment for sensory perception and nervous system development.

claims.claim: Some Atlantic ecotype populations are insensitive to specific lunar time cues, either moonlight or mechanical stimulation by the tides (Kaiser, 2014).
claims.source: Interestingly, some Atlantic ecotype populations are insensitive to specific lunar time cues, either moonlight or mechanical stimulation by the tides (Kaiser, 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claims.claim: Pre-existing insensitivities to lunar time cues may have been combined to form completely insensitive and hence lunar-arrhythmic ecotypes.
claims.source: These pre-existing insensitivities may have been combined to form completely insensitive and hence lunar-arrhythmic ecotypes. This scenario would fit the general pattern of polygenic adaptation through a re-assortment of standing genetic variation, which emerges from our study.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the known variation in the Atlantic ecotype and the pattern of polygenic adaptation observed in this study.

claims.claim: In several species, genes involved in complex behavioral or ecological syndromes were found to be locked into supergenes by chromosomal inversions, for example in Heliconius butterfly mimicry (Joron et al., 2011) or reproductive morphs of the ruff (Küpper et al., 2016).
claims.source: In several species, genes involved in complex behavioral or ecological syndromes were found to be locked into supergenes by chromosomal inversions, for example in Heliconius butterfly mimicry (Joron et al., 2011) or reproductive morphs of the ruff (Küpper et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claims.claim: While a clustering of ecotype-associated alleles is observed in Clunio, there is no obvious connection to an underlying structural variant.
claims.source: While we observe a clustering of ecotype-associated alleles in Clunio, there is no obvious connection to an underlying structural variant (SV).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the lack of evidence for a structural variant in the local PCA analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 9).

claims.claim: Clunio's long history of genome rearrangements (Kaiser et al., 2016) may have resulted in a clustering of ecologically relevant loci without locking them into a single SV.
claims.source: Alternatively, Clunio's long history of genome rearrangements (Kaiser et al., 2016) may have resulted in a clustering of ecologically relevant loci without locking them into a single SV.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the known genome structure of Clunio and the observed clustering of ecotype-associated loci.

claims.claim: Clustering of ecotype-associated loci could be stabilized by low recombination, consistent with the observed three LD blocks.
claims.source: Clustering could be stabilized by low recombination, consistent with the observed three LD blocks, which – while not ecotype-specific – all overlap with the differentiated region.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed LD blocks overlapping with the ecotype-associated region.

claims.claim: Epistatic interactions between the clustered loci and co-adaptation of alleles might further reduce the fitness of recombinants and lead to a concerted response to selection.
claims.source: Epistatic interactions between the clustered loci and co-adaptation of alleles might further reduce the fitness of recombinants and lead to a concerted response to selection.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis about the potential mechanisms maintaining the clustering of ecotype-associated loci.

claims.claim: An interconnected adaptive cluster might allow for more flexible evolutionary responses than a single, completely linked supergene.
claims.source: Such an interconnected adaptive cluster might allow for more flexible evolutionary responses than a single, completely linked supergene.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about the potential evolutionary advantages of the observed genome architecture.

claims.claim: A similar architecture with clustered, tightly linked loci was predicted to result from adaptation with gene flow (Yeaman and Whitlock, 2011).
claims.source: Notably, a similar architecture with clustered, tightly linked loci was predicted to result from adaptation with gene flow (Yeaman and Whitlock, 2011), a scenario which we found in the sympatric Bergen populations.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature and the observation of gene flow in the Bergen populations.

results.result: Clunio midges recolonized Northern Europe after the last glaciation (~10,000 years ago), expanding from a single source into the Baltic Sea and high Arctic, where new ecotypes evolved rapidly in response to local environmental conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C23, C33-C35, C44-C45 collectively establish the postglacial colonization timeline and biogeographic history. The evidence includes geological constraints (C33), subfossil data (C34), mitochondrial haplotype networks showing radiation from a single center (C44), shared nuclear polymorphisms (C44), and nucleotide diversity patterns consistent with expansion fronts (C44). The timeframe of <10,000 years for ecotype evolution is well-supported by converging lines of evidence.

results.result: Three distinct Clunio ecotypes differ in circadian and circalunar timing, oviposition behavior, and habitat use: the Atlantic ecotype is lunar-rhythmic and emerges during spring tide low waters; the Baltic ecotype is lunar-arrhythmic and emerges daily at dusk on open water; and the Arctic ecotype is arrhythmic and emerges at every low tide using a tidal hourglass timer.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C18-C22, C24-C25, C29-C32, C36-C38 describe the phenotypic characteristics of the three ecotypes, supported by laboratory emergence data (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and oviposition behavior observations. The phenotypic characterization is thorough and well-documented, with clear differences among ecotypes confirmed under common garden conditions. The weak lunar rhythm in Ber-2AR (C38) is noted and later explained by gene flow (C51).

results.result: Population genomic analysis reveals strong geographic isolation between sites, but the sympatric Bergen ecotypes (Atlantic Ber-1SL and Baltic Ber-2AR) are genetically very similar with evidence of ongoing gene flow, questioning the species status of C. balticus and suggesting introgression of Baltic ecotype haplotypes into an Atlantic population.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C43, C46-C47 are strongly supported by multiple lines of genomic evidence: PCA showing geographic clustering (Figure 2A-B), mitochondrial haplotype sharing only between Bergen populations (Figure 2D), ADMIXTURE analysis showing separation only at K>6 with admixed individuals (Figure 2C), and TreeMix detecting introgression from Seh-2AR to Ber-2AR (Figure 2E). The convergence of multiple independent analyses provides robust support for ongoing gene flow between sympatric ecotypes.

results.result: Topology weighting analysis reveals rapid changes in tree topologies along chromosomes and massive haplotype sharing across populations, with most haplotype sharing explained by incomplete lineage sorting rather than introgression (only 0.17% of SNPs show introgression signature).
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C49 are supported by topology weighting analysis (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) showing that the genome-wide consensus topology dominates in few windows, and f4 ratio test showing significant but minimal introgression signal (775 SNPs = 0.17% of dataset). The interpretation that incomplete lineage sorting dominates is consistent with recent radiation from a common source. The analytical approach is appropriate for distinguishing these processes.

results.result: QTL mapping of lunar rhythmicity in a Ber-1SL × Ber-2AR cross reveals segregation within and between families but no significant QTL, despite sufficient power to detect the sex-determining locus, indicating lunar rhythmicity has an oligogenic or polygenic basis rather than being controlled by a single large-effect locus.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C54 are supported by crossing data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) showing phenotypic segregation and QTL mapping results (Figure 4) showing no significant QTL for lunar rhythmicity but clear detection of the sex-determining locus as a positive control. The inference of polygenic architecture is reasonable given the power analysis. However, the authors acknowledge limitations including limited markers (n=23), sample size (n=272), and phenotyping error where arrhythmic individuals emerging at peak days are scored as rhythmic.

results.result: Genome-wide association analysis identifies ecotype-associated variants distributed across the genome with a concentration on chromosome 1, but genetic differentiation is extremely low between ecotypes (no diagnostic variants, only 63 SNPs with FST≥0.75), and the chromosome 1 cluster is not associated with a structural variant, indicating numerous loci contribute to ecotype differences without being differentially fixed.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C64 are supported by multiple complementary analyses: XtX and eBPmc statistics showing genome-wide distribution with chromosome 1 enrichment (Figure 3B-C), control analyses with environmental variables showing specificity (C56, Figure 3—figure supplement 3D-E), FST analysis showing extremely low differentiation (C57-C58, Figure 3D-E), LD analysis showing blocks that don't correspond to ecotype-associated regions (C59-C60, Figure 3—figure supplement 8), and local PCA showing no structural variant signature (C61, Figure 3—figure supplement 9). The convergence of evidence strongly supports a polygenic architecture without large-effect loci.

results.result: 82% of ecotype-associated SNPs are polymorphic in both Atlantic and Baltic ecotypes, and 90% of Northern European ecotype-associated alleles are also segregating in southern populations (Vigo, St. Jean-de-Luz), indicating adaptation primarily involves standing genetic variation rather than new mutations.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C66 are supported by direct analysis of allele sharing among ecotype-associated SNPs (eBPmc>3, XtX>threshold). The high proportion of shared polymorphisms (82% between ecotypes, 90% with southern populations) provides strong evidence for adaptation from standing variation. The comparison with southern populations is particularly compelling as these are potential source populations for postglacial colonization. The analysis appropriately excludes Bergen populations to avoid confounding by ongoing gene flow.

results.result: GO term enrichment analysis of genes harboring ecotype-associated variants reveals strong enrichment for circadian clock genes (3 of top 4 GO terms) and nervous system development, with additional enrichment for ecdysteroid metabolism, imaginal disc development, and gonad development, but striking absence of metabolic and immune system processes, suggesting ecotypes are primarily defined by changes in circadian timing and nervous system development.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C72 are supported by comprehensive GO term enrichment analysis (Figure 5) using appropriate statistical methods (topGO with weight01 Fisher's exact test) and a well-defined gene universe (5,393 genes with GO terms from 15,193 confidence gene models). The clustering analysis (Figure 5B-C) shows that circadian GO terms are driven by core clock genes and nervous system development involves nearly half the genes. The absence of metabolic/immune enrichment despite many annotated genes (2,634 and 185 respectively) strengthens the specificity of the findings. The congruence with known ecotype differences supports the biological interpretation.

results.result: The 13 most strongly ecotype-associated genes (FST≥0.75, eBPmc>10) in 8 genomic regions include genes involved in circadian timing (sNPF-R, Mmp1), sensory perception (cOps1, lola), nervous system development (tll), and other processes, reflecting all major biological processes from GO term analysis, but show only mild reductions in genetic diversity and mild increases in LD, indicating very soft selection consistent with polygenic adaptation from standing variation.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C77 are supported by stringent filtering for top candidates (Figure 6A) and analysis of selective sweep signatures (Figure 6B-G). The candidate genes are biologically plausible and include functionally relevant loci (e.g., sNPF-R couples emergence to circadian clock, Mmp1 processes PDF neuropeptide). The lack of strong selective sweep signatures (mild diversity reduction, mild LD increase) at the most differentiated loci is consistent with soft selection and polygenic adaptation. However, the interpretation relies on absence of evidence rather than evidence of absence, which is inherently weaker.

results.result: Genomic analysis confirms recent ecotype establishment with massive haplotype sharing, and QTL mapping plus genome screens reveal polygenic adaptation from standing genetic variation involving circadian clock genes, sensory perception genes, and nervous system development genes, demonstrating that adaptive ecotype formation occurred rapidly with ongoing gene flow based on re-assortment of existing alleles.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C6 represent the main conclusions synthesizing multiple lines of evidence from the study. C3 is supported by haplotype sharing data (C48-C49, Figure 2-3), C4 by QTL mapping (C52-C54, Figure 4) and genome-wide association (C55-C64, Figure 3), C5 by GO enrichment and candidate gene analyses (C68-C75, Figures 5-6), and C6 by the combination of low differentiation (C57-C58), shared polymorphisms (C65-C66), ongoing gene flow in Bergen (C42), and postglacial timeframe (C45). The convergence of independent analytical approaches provides strong support for these integrative conclusions.

results.result: The Baltic and Atlantic ecotypes were previously reported to co-occur sympatrically near Bergen in temporal reproductive isolation, leading to classification of the Baltic ecotype as a separate species (C. balticus), though the two can be successfully interbred in the laboratory.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C28 accurately report prior work by Heimbach (1978) on sympatric occurrence, temporal isolation, species status, and laboratory interbreeding. These are factual statements about previous research and taxonomic classification, supported by appropriate citations. The current study's genomic data (C42-C43) questions this species status, but the claims about prior work are accurately stated.

results.result: Prior work has established that quantitative traits typically have polygenic basis, rapid adaptation should occur via subtle allele frequency changes at many loci, examples of polygenic adaptation exist in humans and other species, but powerful datasets are limited and examples in natural populations are rare, with theoretical predictions about genetic architecture differing under scenarios with versus without gene flow.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C14 accurately summarize relevant prior literature on polygenic adaptation, citing appropriate sources (Sella and Barton 2019, Boyle et al. 2017, Turchin et al. 2012, Barghi et al. 2020, Kautt et al. 2020, Yeaman and Whitlock 2011, Orr 1998). These claims establish the theoretical and empirical context for the study. The citations appear appropriate and the characterizations of prior work are reasonable, though the reviewer cannot verify all cited claims without consulting the original sources.

results.result: Circalunar clocks are biological time-keeping mechanisms that allow organisms to anticipate lunar phase, their molecular basis is unknown, and in Clunio marinus they synchronize reproduction and have additional ecological relevance.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C17 accurately describe circalunar clocks and cite appropriate sources (Neumann 2014, Andreatta and Tessmar-Raible 2020, Kaiser 2014). These are factual statements about established biological phenomena that provide context for the study. The characterization that the molecular basis is unknown (C16) is important for motivating the genomic approach to identifying adaptive loci.

results.result: 168 field-caught individuals from six geographic sites were sequenced for full nuclear and mitochondrial genomes.
results.evaluation: Claim C39 describes the genomic dataset that forms the foundation of the study. This is supported by the methods section describing DNA extraction, library preparation, and sequencing at 15-20x coverage. The sample size (24 individuals per population, with minor variations) and sequencing approach are appropriate for population genomic analysis. Raw data deposition at ENA (PRJEB43766) supports reproducibility.

results.result: GO terms for 'male courtship behavior', 'inter-male aggression' and 'copulation' highlight a previously unknown aspect of Clunio ecotype formation that could lead to assortative mating between ecotypes.
results.evaluation: Claim C73 identifies enriched GO terms related to sexual selection and mating behavior (Figure 5) and speculates about potential for assortative mating. While the GO term enrichment is data-supported, the interpretation as a 'previously unknown aspect' and the speculation about future assortative mating is not directly tested. The claim appropriately uses cautious language ('could in the long term entail'), but represents speculation rather than demonstrated findings. Additional behavioral studies would be needed to test this hypothesis.

results.result: Deep genomic analysis allowed reconstruction of detailed biogeographic history, revealing that sympatric ecotypes previously considered different species are the most closely related populations, and that ecotype-associated alleles are largely shared between ecotypes, suggesting adaptation from standing genetic variation at many loci.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C80 are summary statements synthesizing major findings. C78 is supported by the comprehensive population genomic analyses (C40-C49), C79 by the Bergen population data (C42-C43, Figure 2), and C80 by the allele sharing analyses (C65-C66). These represent appropriate high-level conclusions from the data, though they are somewhat redundant with other results already evaluated.

results.result: Similar re-use of regulatory variation has been found in sticklebacks and Heliconius butterflies, though in Heliconius alleles are shared via introgression over large evolutionary distances while Clunio ecotypes diverged recently from a common source; the ancestral Atlantic ecotype comprises many genetically determined circadian timing types adapted to local tides.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C83 compare the current findings to prior work and describe the ancestral Atlantic ecotype. C81-C82 cite appropriate comparative examples (Chan et al. 2010, Edelman et al. 2019) and correctly distinguish the Clunio pattern (recent divergence with shared polymorphism) from Heliconius (ancient introgression). C83 accurately describes prior work on Atlantic ecotype variation (Kaiser 2014, Neumann 1967, Kaiser et al. 2016, 2021). These contextual claims are well-supported by citations.

results.result: Existing genetic variants for dusk emergence were likely selected or re-assorted to form the Baltic ecotype's concentrated dusk emergence, and good congruence between phenotypic differences and detected biological processes could be a hallmark of polygenic adaptation.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C85 represent speculative interpretations. C84 proposes a plausible mechanism for Baltic ecotype evolution based on known Atlantic variation, but this is not directly tested. C85 proposes a general principle about polygenic adaptation based on the observed congruence in this study, but this represents a hypothesis rather than a demonstrated finding. Both claims use appropriate cautious language ('likely', 'could be'), but represent speculation that would require additional studies to validate.

results.result: Three hypotheses are proposed for molecular pathways involved in the circalunar clock: (1) lunar arrhythmicity may involve escape from circalunar control of ecdysteroid-dependent development; (2) circalunar clocks may involve circadian clocks, so circadian changes could affect both circadian and circalunar rhythms; (3) sensory receptor development/sensitivity may differ between ecotypes, and pre-existing insensitivities to specific lunar cues may have been combined to form completely insensitive ecotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C93 propose three mechanistic hypotheses for circalunar clock function and evolution. C86, C88, C90, C92 cite relevant prior work establishing context. C87, C89, C91, C93 propose hypotheses based on the GO term enrichment and candidate gene findings. While these are plausible hypotheses consistent with the data, they represent speculation about mechanisms rather than demonstrated findings. The hypotheses are appropriately presented as possibilities ('may', 'might', 'could'), but would require functional studies to test. The speculation is reasonable given the data but remains unvalidated.

results.result: While clustering of ecotype-associated alleles is observed on chromosome 1, there is no obvious connection to a structural variant; possible explanations include historical genome rearrangements creating clustering without a single SV, stabilization by low recombination and LD blocks, and epistatic interactions reducing recombinant fitness, potentially allowing more flexible evolutionary responses than a completely linked supergene, consistent with theoretical predictions for adaptation with gene flow.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C100 discuss the chromosome 1 clustering and propose alternative explanations. C94 accurately cites examples of supergenes (Joron et al. 2011, Küpper et al. 2016). C95 is supported by lack of SV signature in local PCA (Figure 3—figure supplement 9). C96-C99 propose speculative mechanisms (historical rearrangements, low recombination, epistasis, flexible responses) that are plausible but not directly tested. C100 notes consistency with theory (Yeaman and Whitlock 2011) and observation of gene flow in Bergen. The speculation is reasonable but the mechanisms remain hypothetical and would require additional studies to validate.
